tagline: A desert highway whose river crossing moved before the Bicentennial paving
intro: Highway 95 runs from Hanksville through canyon country to US 191 south of Blanding, a paved journey of 121 miles. Utah designates SR-95 between SR-24 and US 191 as the Bicentennial Highway Scenic Byway. Visit Utah’s description of the Bicentennial Highway Scenic Byway emphasizes the Henry Mountains to the west and rugged canyons leading toward Hite Crossing. Below the Ticaboo fork, the road winds between carved, pockmarked redrock walls. The tourism office allows half a day with few stops and a brief visit to Natural Bridges, or a full day with hiking. Capitol Reef Country highlights North Wash’s sheer canyon walls and the Colorado River crossing as defining features of the drive.

SR-95 entered the state system in 1935 as a spur from near Blanding to Natural Bridges National Monument. In 1949 it extended across the Colorado at Hite to Hanksville. Except for a short section near Blanding, the route remained unpaved through the 1960s. Lake Powell’s flooding required a new alignment and river crossing, completed in 1966. Paving for the 1976 US Bicentennial gave the highway its lasting name.

Heading south from Hanksville, pass Little Egypt and continue toward Hog Springs and Hite. Beyond the river crossing come Fry Canyon, the Natural Bridges turnoff, and the archaeological sites at Mule Canyon and Butler Wash. SR-95 ends at US 191, 4.3 miles south of Blanding.

moments.title: Little Egypt
moments.text: Visit Utah identifies the large mesa on the right when traveling south from Hanksville as Little Egypt. Its account credits early cowboys with the name: the formation reminded them of the Egyptian Sphinx. Capitol Reef Country also points travelers toward Little Egypt’s redrock hoodoos south of town. The Henry Mountains lie west of the highway, with Mount Ellen appearing before Mount Pennell on the southbound drive.
moments.notice: Look west toward the Henry Mountains: southbound, Mount Ellen comes first, followed by Mount Pennell.

moments.title: Hite Crossing Bridge
moments.text: Hite Crossing’s arch carries SR-95 across the Colorado River upstream of an older ford and ferry route. In 1880, prospector Cass Hite established Dandy Crossing near the mouth of the Dirty Devil River. The old ford lay two miles downstream from the present bridge, near the mouth of the Dirty Devil River. Arthur Chaffin added an automobile ferry in 1946, powered by an old car engine and held by a steel cable. The ferry ran for twenty years before Lake Powell inundated Hite. The bridge belonged to a highway realignment prompted by the reservoir, and was dedicated on June 3, 1966.

moments.title: Fry Canyon
moments.text: Fry Canyon grew during the uranium boom of the 1950s and is now a ghost town. The former community lies just south of White Canyon, along State Route 95. Its lodge opened in 1955 and closed in 2007. Mining left consequences beyond the settlement: a uranium mill and later copper operation at Fry Spring contaminated groundwater in Fry Creek’s channel deposits. The US Geological Survey installed three barriers containing different reactive materials at the site, which the Bureau of Land Management manages. Beyond Fry Canyon, Visit Utah describes sparse juniper and pinyon cover on the approach to Natural Bridges.
